newsitem.title: USA: Los Angeles transit plan may fall $1.3 bln short.
newsitem.headline: Los Angeles transit plan may fall $1.3 bln short.

text.p: The Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority's long-range transit plan may contain a $1.3 billion shortfall, California state Auditor Kurt Sjoberg said on Wednesday.

Certain aspects of the Los Angeles authority's $72.5 billion long-range plan "appear flawed," the state auditor said in a report. Sjoberg said the plan may contain a $1.3 billion shortfall due to an "optimistic inflation forecast and anticipated cost efficiencies unlikely to materialize."
The Los Angeles agency, established in 1993 by state law, is the second largest public transit authority in the nation.

The authority coordinates the operation of all public transportation services within Los Angeles County, including long-range regional transportation planning, light and heavy commuter rail systems and bus service.
The auditor's report was presented Wednesday to Gov. Pete Wilson and legislative leaders.

The report said the Los Angeles authority's projected financial results for fiscal year 1995-1996 exceeded its revised operating budget by about $14 million. In addition, revenue and expense trends indicated that the agency's deficit reduction plan "did not appear realistic," the report said.
The Los Angeles authority has asserted that, when final financial information is available for fiscal year 1995-1996, the deficit will have been eliminated, the state auditor said.

When it formulated its fiscal year 1996-1997 budget, the state auditor said the Los Angeles authority anticipated significant operating cost reductions. But the state audit concluded that those reductions were unlikely to materialize.

"If the cost reductions do not occur, the (authority) will incur an operating deficit greater than that of the previous fiscal year when the carryover deficit from fiscal year 1995-1996 is considered," the auditor's report said.
The Los Angeles authority's outstanding long-term debt came to about $3.1 billion as of June 30, 1996, with annual debt service requirements of about $230 million.
The authority's plan to manage its debt includes the issuance of bonds totaling more than $2 billion over the next several years.
"The debt management plan complies with prescribed limits imposed by its trustees and with a self-imposed policy related to refunding bonds," the state auditor said.
